articles.title: Petrol Supply Concerns Rise as Marketers Await Clarity on Dangote Refinery’s Dollar Pricing Plan
articles.description: Bimpe Aremu Uncertainty has continued to ripple through Nigeria's downstream petroleum sector as petroleum marketers scale back fuel purchases while awaiting clarity over the Dangote Petroleum Refinery's new pricing structure, raising concerns about possible disruptions in fuel distribution across the country. The development follows reports that marketers have reduced large-scale loading of Premium Motor Spirit (PMS), popularly known as petrol, after the refinery adopted a dollar-based pricing template for some transactions. Although speculation emerged that loading activities had been suspended at the Lekki-based refinery, officials of the Dangote Group have dismissed the claim, insisting that product loading is still ongoing. Marketers Adopt Wait-and-See Approach Petroleum marketers say the uncertainty surrounding the refinery's pricing policy has forced many operators to suspend fresh purchases until there is a clearer understanding of the market direction. The National Publicity Secretary of the Independent Petroleum Marketers Association of Nigeria (IPMAN), Chinedu Ukadike, explained that marketers are reluctant to commit huge sums to fuel purchases because they cannot predict whether prices will rise or fall after buying. "The issue is simple; marketers are not buying because they are trying to look at the market dynamics. Whatever we are using today is existing products in tank farms, which we are buying around N1,250 and N1,300." Ukadike noted that the uncertainty has been compounded by expectations surrounding new crude supplies and imported petroleum products, whose eventual pricing remains unknown. "The problem we are now facing is that this new crude oil that they are bringing—what will be the template? Also, those who have brought in petroleum products and are given licences are also estimated to place their price at N1,350, which marketers are also wary of." According to him, marketers fear purchasing products at current prices only to suffer losses if petrol becomes cheaper shortly afterwards. "So everyone is just sceptical about loading products because when you load, you don't know the next price, if it is going to reduce or go higher. You are still expected by consumers to sell at the prevailing price." While he stressed that fuel distribution has not completely stopped, he admitted that the volume of products being loaded has dropped considerably. Ukadike also urged the Federal Government to urgently resolve the pricing dispute to restore confidence in the downstream market. "The Federal Government has to look inward and resolve this issue once and for all. This template issue should be resolved immediately." South-West Marketers Report Reduced Supply Several marketers in the South-West also confirmed that the uncertainty has forced many filling station operators to suspend fresh purchases. IPMAN Western Zone Chairman, Oyewole Akanni, told the News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) that the situation began after petrol loading reportedly stopped at the Dangote refinery about four days earlier. According to him, marketers have since turned to private depots where prices are significantly higher. He disclosed that ex-depot prices in Lagos currently range between N1,200 and N1,220 per litre, excluding transportation costs, while some marketers paid between N1,210 and N1,220 per litre for supplies purchased on Friday. "The non-availability of fuel at some filling stations and the closure of others are due to fluctuations in the price of lifting fuel from depots." Akanni added that many marketers whose existing stock had been exhausted were deliberately waiting to see whether prices would fall when Dangote resumes full sales or increase further. "Since the Dangote refinery stopped selling PMS about four days ago, private depot owners have increased their prices. Many filling stations that have exhausted their stock are waiting to see whether prices will come down when the Dangote refinery resumes sales or increase further. Only a few marketers are buying products for now because of the uncertainty." Despite the situation, he maintained that Nigeria was not experiencing fuel scarcity and advised motorists against panic buying. "There is no fuel scarcity. Members of the public should not panic. Although there is a possibility of an increase in the pump price if the current situation persists." Akanni also claimed that several trucks meant to load products at the refinery had remained idle. "I was supposed to have received four truckloads of PMS four days ago, but that has not happened because the trucks are at the Dangote refinery, which has not been selling. The company is not even loading its own trucks. They are all parked there." He further observed that even the Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited (NNPC Ltd.) had been affected because it also sources products from the refinery. Dangote Refinery Rejects Suspension Claims The Dangote Group has strongly denied reports that fuel loading has been suspended. A company spokesman described the reports as "fake news" and insisted that loading operations remain active. "The refinery is loading. Anybody can go there to check. That's fake news to say we are not loading." The official also argued that marketers importing petrol are struggling to compete because rising fuel prices in Lomé, Togo, have made imported products less competitive compared to locally refined fuel. Behind the Federal Government and Dangote Disagreement Sources familiar with ongoing discussions between the Federal Government and Dangote Petroleum Refinery say negotiations are continuing over issues that led to the refinery's decision to adopt a dollar-based pricing model. According to a senior government official who spoke anonymously because of the sensitive nature of the talks, the disagreement extends beyond petrol pricing. The source said the refinery is dissatisfied with two major issues: the Federal Government's continued approval of petrol import licences despite its refining capacity, and what it considers inadequate crude oil supply—particularly the relatively small proportion of crude sold in naira. "So the issue is that Dangote is unhappy about two things; one is that the government gave import permits... Then number two is that the refinery is saying that it is not getting enough crude oil even from the Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited." The official explained that because a significant portion of crude purchases must still be made in dollars, the refinery believes pricing refined products in dollars has become necessary. Government officials, however, insist they cannot restrict imports simply to satisfy one market participant. "If there is no agreement and he does not want to listen, the next step will be to allow more imports to come in. It is not possible to hold anybody to ransom." The official also noted that the refinery's location within a Free Trade Zone gives it flexibility to conduct commercial transactions in foreign currency. FCCPC Insists Naira Remains Legal Tender Amid reports that petroleum products may be priced in dollars, the Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (FCCPC) reaffirmed that the Nigerian naira remains the country's only legal tender for domestic commercial transactions. FCCPC Director of Corporate Affairs, Ondaje Ijagwu, said: "The commission's position is clear. The Nigerian naira is the legal tender in Nigeria and remains the lawful currency for domestic commercial transactions." The commission also expressed concern that reductions in global crude oil prices have not translated into corresponding reductions in petrol prices across Nigeria. According to Ijagwu, consumers deserve to benefit from declining international oil prices whenever market conditions support such adjustments. "The FCCPC remains concerned that recent declines in international crude oil prices have not been reflected proportionately in retail petrol prices." He added that the commission would continue monitoring developments and would not hesitate to act where there is evidence of anti-competitive practices or consumer exploitation. Court Challenge Adds Another Twist Complicating the matter further, three major oil marketing companies—Matrix Energy Group, AA Rano Nigeria and AYM Shafa Holdings—have reportedly approached the Federal High Court seeking an order compelling regulators to continue issuing licences for petroleum product imports. The marketers argue that they have invested billions of dollars in storage, logistics and distribution infrastructure and should not be prevented from importing fuel while legal and commercial uncertainties remain. Government officials say the legal action limits their ability to halt imports entirely, even as discussions with Dangote Refinery continue. For now, industry stakeholders remain hopeful that ongoing negotiations between the Federal Government and the refinery will produce a lasting solution capable of stabilising fuel prices, restoring confidence among marketers and preventing unnecessary disruptions in Nigeria's petroleum supply chain.
